youtube.title: How Nokia Lost Its Empire
youtube.description:
Test upload from an automated pipeline. In 2007 Nokia sold roughly half of all smartphones on Earth - then the iPhone arrived.

Facts in this test script are illustrative and not yet fact-checked.

paragraphs.text: In 2007, Nokia sold roughly half of all the smartphones on Earth.
Its phones were in pockets from Helsinki to Jakarta.

shots.query: busy city street crowd people walking

paragraphs.text: It began in Finland, home to about five and a half million people.
Founded in 1865 as a paper mill, it reinvented itself again and again.

shots.prompt: 19th century Finnish paper mill beside a river in winter, wooden buildings, smoke rising, dramatic light

paragraphs.text: By the late nineties, it was the world's biggest phone maker.
At its peak, half of all smartphones sold carried its name.
Then, in 2007, Apple launched the iPhone.

shots.query: hand using smartphone touchscreen close up

paragraphs.text: Nokia's phones still sold, but its software could not keep up.

shots.prompt: an old generic candybar mobile phone with a green screen on a dark table, moody low key light, shallow depth of field

paragraphs.text: In 2011, its new chief executive told his staff the company had fallen behind.

shots.quote: We have fallen behind, we have missed big trends, and we have lost time.
shots.author: Stephen Elop, 2011

paragraphs.text: In 2013, Microsoft bought the phone business for 5.4 billion euros.
This is how an empire lost its way.
